Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Vignette:
Martin Weber is a 55-year-old single white American man who works as a counselor, and when he describes the day that still organizes his life, he does so in fragments that circle around smell, sound, and the sudden sense that ordinary objects can become dangerous without warning. He had been in a public office building during a man-made disaster that ended in fire. What stays closest to him is not a clean sequence of images but the moment the atmosphere changed: something hurled across the room, the crack of impact, people shouting, and then the sharp, burnt smell that spread so fast it seemed to enter his throat and lungs before he understood what was happening. Smoke followed quickly. In his memory, the danger is inseparable from thrown objects and the smell of burning; those details still feel to him like the first unmistakable signs that life can turn violent in an instant.

In the aftermath, Martin returned to work outwardly composed, the way many of his clients expected him to be. As a counselor, he was used to listening carefully and presenting steadiness, and for a time he tried to treat his own reactions as something to manage privately. Yet in session or while walking through the office, he found himself reacting to small moments that others barely noticed. If someone tossed a file onto a desk, dropped a pen sharply into a trash can, or flung a backpack into a chair, his whole body tightened before he could think. If he passed a break room with scorched popcorn or caught even a faint smoke or burnt odor from outside, he was abruptly back in the atmosphere of that day. Sometimes he did not even see the event in his mind. Instead, the fear arrived at full force without a clear picture, as if the emotion had outrun memory. At other times, when he allowed himself to think about what had happened, he could smell again what he had smelled then, so vividly that it seemed to be happening in the present.

What unsettled Martin almost as much as the memories themselves was the strangeness of them. He would describe the event and then stop, saying it felt as though he were talking about something that had happened to someone else. The memory felt alien to him, detached from the person he believed himself to be. This disconnection did not reassure him. It frightened him. He had come to believe that his body was acting like an enemy, launching him into alarm even when he was objectively safe in his office, at home, or driving to work. He monitored himself constantly for signs that he might be losing control or “going crazy,” checking his thoughts for anything that suggested he was slipping. If his mind drifted near the disaster, he pulled it away quickly. He was certain that if he let himself think about it directly, he would not be able to handle what came up.

Over months, this caution narrowed his life. Martin stopped seeing friends as often, usually declining invitations with plausible excuses about work or fatigue. The effort of keeping himself composed all week left little room for social contact, and being around other people brought too many unpredictable moments—someone throwing their keys onto a counter, a backyard fire pit, the smell of a grill slightly overlit, a joking gesture that involved tossing an object across a room. At work he became more aware than ever of the environment around him. He noticed every smell in the building, every sudden movement, every sound that might signal the beginning of something dangerous. He had come to believe that he needed to be especially careful at all times because you never know what can happen next. That idea felt less like a thought than a rule for survival.

The strain of living this way became harder to hide. In counseling sessions, he sometimes lost track of what clients were saying when a burnt smell drifted in from the street or a colleague dropped something in the hallway. He worried about what his clients saw in him in those moments: the pause, the fixed attention to the door, the split second in which he was no longer fully with them. He was ashamed that he, of all people, could not simply reason his way through it.

Martin finally sought help after recognizing how small his life had become and how much effort went into preventing his own mind from approaching the disaster. He is frightened that if he stops avoiding the memory, the emotional force of it will overwhelm him completely. At the same time, he hopes for something simple and profound: to sit in his office, smell burnt coffee or hear something hit the floor, and remain in the present rather than feeling his body and mind carried somewhere else.
